description_full: First Majestic Silver Corp. engages in the acquisition, exploration, development, and production of mineral properties in North America. The company explores for silver and gold deposits. Its projects include the San Dimas silver/gold mine covering an area of approximately 71,867 hectares located in Durango State, Mexico; the Santa Elena silver/gold mine that covers an area of approximately 102,244 hectares located in Sonora State, Mexico; the Los Gatos Silver Mine covering an area of approximately 103,000 hectares located in Chihuahua, Mexico; and the La Encantada silver mine that covers an area of approximately 4,076 hectares located in Coahuila State, Mexico. The company was formerly known as First Majestic Resource Corp. and changed its name to First Majestic Silver Corp. in November 2006. First Majestic Silver Corp. was incorporated in 1979 and is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada.

financial_summary: First Majestic Silver Corp. is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $7.5B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +26% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +7.5pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at -0% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 6% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $464M in free cash flow — roughly 37 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 15× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.1%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
